title: "The chi-squared distribution"
execute:
  enabled: true

The normal page estimated a mean and [variance](variance-and-covariance.qmd) for each /i/ F1 speaker group. Under an [independent](../foundations/independence.qmd) normal-sampling model, the uncertainty in an estimated variance has a **chi-squared reference distribution**.

We construct that reference statistic, connect its degrees of freedom to the number of centered vowel measurements, and then use the resulting density to interpret variance uncertainty under the normal model.

## Definition

If $Z_1,\ldots,Z_\nu$ are independent standard-normal variables, then

$$
Q=\sum_{j=1}^{\nu}Z_j^2
\sim\chi^2_\nu.
$$

Its density is

$$
f_Q(q)
=\frac{q^{\nu/2-1}e^{-q/2}}
       {2^{\nu/2}\Gamma(\nu/2)},
\qquad q>0.
$$

The [gamma function introduced with the beta
distribution](beta-distribution.qmd#gamma-function-and-recurrence) extends the
factorial operation to positive noninteger inputs. Here it supplies the
normalizing constant even when $\nu/2$ is not an integer, so that the area
under the chi-squared density is one. Its mean and variance are

$$
\mathbb{E}[Q]=\nu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[Q]=2\nu.
$$

The moments follow from independence and the standard-normal moments:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[Q]
&=\sum_{j=1}^{\nu}\mathbb{E}[Z_j^2]
=\nu,\\
\operatorname{Var}[Q]
&=\sum_{j=1}^{\nu}\operatorname{Var}[Z_j^2]
=2\nu.
\end{aligned}
$$

The remaining question is why estimating the mean leaves only $n-1$
independent deviations. We can see the constraint before introducing the
general result. The values $320$, $350$, and $380$ Hz have mean $350$ Hz and
centered deviations

$$
(-30,0,30).
$$

These three deviations must add to zero. Once the first two have been chosen,
the third is fixed: $30=-(-30+0)$. We began with three measurements, used one
quantity to estimate their mean, and retained two freely varying deviations.
The same argument leaves $n-1$ freely varying deviations in a sample of size
$n$.

How does that counting argument connect to the chi-squared construction? Think
of the $n$ observations as the coordinates of one point in an $n$-dimensional
space. The direction
$\mathbf 1=(1,\ldots,1)$ moves every coordinate together and thus changes the
sample mean. A **projection** is the component, or shadow, of a vector along a
chosen direction. Two directions are **orthogonal** when they are
perpendicular, equivalently when their dot product is zero.
The earlier [vector and matrix
primer](variance-and-covariance.qmd#vectors-matrices-and-covariance) defines a
vector as an ordered tuple and a dot product as paired multiplication followed
by addition.

A **residual** is a centered observation $X_i-\overline X$; the later
[residual page](../regression-models/residuals.qmd) develops the same
observed-minus-fitted idea for regression. The **residual subspace** is the
collection of all centered vectors whose coordinates sum to zero. Every such
vector is orthogonal to $\mathbf 1$, because
$\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}(d_1,\ldots,d_n)=\sum_i d_i=0$. It has $n-1$
freely varying directions: after $n-1$ deviations have been chosen, the
zero-sum constraint fixes the last one.

The two-coordinate case lets us draw the decomposition. The diagonal line is
the mean direction: moving along it changes both coordinates together. The
other line is the residual subspace: its coordinates sum to zero. The blue
arrow is the observed vector's projection onto the mean direction, and the
red arrow is the remaining residual component.

```{r}
#| label: plot-mean-residual-projection
#| fig-cap: "A two-coordinate vector decomposed into orthogonal mean and residual components."
#| fig-alt: "A coordinate plane shows the mean direction y equals x and the perpendicular residual direction y equals minus x. An observed vector from the origin is decomposed into a blue arrow along the mean direction and a red arrow parallel to the residual direction. The two components meet at a right angle."
library(ggplot2)

projection_point <- data.frame(
  mean_x = 1.2, # dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
  mean_y = 1.2, # dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
  observed_x = 1.8, # dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
  observed_y = 0.6 # dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
)

ggplot() +
  geom_abline(
    slope = 1, intercept = 0,
    color = "#2C7FB8", linewidth = 0.65
  ) +
  geom_abline(
    slope = -1, intercept = 0,
    color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.65
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    data = projection_point,
    aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = observed_x, yend = observed_y),
    color = "grey45", linetype = "dashed", # dqr-allow: plot-aesthetic
    arrow = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(0.12, "inches"))
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    data = projection_point,
    aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = mean_x, yend = mean_y),
    color = "#2C7FB8", linewidth = 0.9, # dqr-allow: plot-aesthetic
    arrow = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(0.12, "inches"))
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    data = projection_point,
    aes(x = mean_x, y = mean_y, xend = observed_x, yend = observed_y),
    color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.9, # dqr-allow: plot-aesthetic
    arrow = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(0.12, "inches"))
  ) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.68, y = 1.82, label = "mean direction", color = "#2C7FB8", size = 3.3) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.58, y = -1.72, label = "residual subspace", color = "#8B1A1A", size = 3.3) +
  annotate("point", x = 1.8, y = 0.6, size = 2) + # dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
  annotate("text", x = 1.86, y = 0.45, label = "observed vector", hjust = 0, size = 3.2) +
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(-0.25, 2.25), ylim = c(-2, 2.05), clip = "off") +
  labs(x = "Coordinate 1", y = "Coordinate 2") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The right angle is the geometric meaning of orthogonality. For more than two
observations, the residual subspace has more directions, but the same
projection idea applies.

Our three-value residual vector $(-30,0,30)$ lies in a two-dimensional
residual subspace of the three-coordinate space. Its projection in the mean
direction is zero because its coordinates add to zero.

Now standardize the sample as $Z_i=(X_i-\mu)/\sigma$. The total standardized
sum of squares decomposes into the squared length of the residual projection
and the squared length of the mean projection:

$$
\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\frac{X_i-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2
=\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\frac{X_i-\overline X}{\sigma}\right)^2
+n\left(\frac{\overline X-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2.
$$

The left side is a sum of $n$ independent squared standard normals. Under
normal sampling, the projection onto the sample-mean direction and the
projection onto the residual subspace are independent. The mean component uses
one dimension, leaving an $(n-1)$-dimensional residual component. Since

$$
\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\frac{X_i-\overline X}{\sigma}\right)^2
=\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2},
$$

that component has the $\chi^2_{n-1}$ distribution. We have thus obtained the
variance result:

$$
\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2_{n-1}
$$

for an independent sample from $\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)$. In the
three-observation example, the corresponding standardized squared residual
length has a $\chi^2_2$ reference distribution. The conclusion depends on
independent normal sampling: orthogonality by itself does not guarantee
independence for an arbitrary distribution.

## Degrees of freedom from the vowel data

For each speaker group below, the degrees of freedom equal one less than the
number of speakers who produced /i/ in the [Hillenbrand
dataset](continuous-random-variables.qmd). The observed group sizes thus
determine the reference distributions.

```{r}
#| label: hillenbrand-chi-square
library(ggplot2)

vowels <- read.csv(
  "data/hillenbrand/vowels-complete.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
i_tokens <- subset(vowels, vowel == "i")
group_sizes <- as.data.frame(table(i_tokens$speaker_type), responseName = "n")
names(group_sizes)[1] <- "speaker_type"
group_sizes$df <- group_sizes$n - 1L
group_sizes$reference_mean <- group_sizes$df
group_sizes$reference_variance <- 2 * group_sizes$df

chi_grid <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(group_sizes)), function(j) {
  df <- group_sizes$df[j]
  q <- seq(0, qchisq(0.999, df), length.out = 400L)
  data.frame(speaker_type = group_sizes$speaker_type[j], df = df,
             q = q, density = dchisq(q, df))
}))

adult_men <- subset(group_sizes, speaker_type == "man")
adult_men_interval <- qchisq(c(0.025, 0.975), df = adult_men$df)

stopifnot(
  sum(group_sizes$n) == 139L,
  all(group_sizes$df == group_sizes$n - 1L),
  all(group_sizes$reference_variance == 2 * group_sizes$reference_mean)
)

group_sizes
adult_men_interval
```

For adult men, $\nu=$ `r adult_men$df`. The reference mean is thus `r adult_men$reference_mean` and the reference variance is `r adult_men$reference_variance`. The central reference interval runs from `r sprintf("%.2f", adult_men_interval[1])` to `r sprintf("%.2f", adult_men_interval[2])`.

```{r}
#| label: plot-hillenbrand-chi-square
#| fig-cap: "Chi-squared reference densities whose degrees of freedom come from the observed /i/ speaker-group sizes."
ggplot(chi_grid, aes(q, density, group = speaker_type,
                     linetype = speaker_type, color = speaker_type)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_color_grey(start = 0.2, end = 0.7) +
  labs(x = expression(chi^2), y = "Reference density",
       color = "Speaker group", linetype = "Speaker group") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

There is deliberately no observed chi-squared statistic in this plot. Computing $(n-1)S^2/\sigma^2$ requires a specified population variance $\sigma^2$, and the dataset does not supply one. The curves show how the reference changes with an empirically determined sample size; later inference pages will use that reference to reason about an unknown variance.

Keep three objects separate. $Q=\sum_{j=1}^{\nu}Z_j^2$ is the abstract random
construction. $(n-1)S^2/\sigma^2$ is the random variance statistic under a
normal-sampling model. A realized value $q$ can be computed only after both the
sample and the candidate $\sigma^2$ are specified.

## Check your understanding

1. Confirm each degree of freedom from the raw /i/ rows.
2. Why does the variance statistic use $n-1$ degrees of freedom?
3. Use `qchisq()` to compute the corresponding central interval for another speaker group.
4. Why would substituting the sample variance for $\sigma^2$ erase the inferential question?
5. Which assumption licenses independence of the mean and residual components
   in the projection argument?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The raw /i/ groups contain 27 boys, 19 girls, 45 men, and 48 women, giving 26, 18, 44, and 47 degrees of freedom, respectively. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The variance statistic has $n-1$ degrees of freedom because estimating the sample mean imposes the constraint that the centered deviations sum to zero. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. For the 48 women, `qchisq(c(.025, .975), df = 47)` gives the central interval $[29.956,67.821]$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Replacing $\sigma^2$ with the same sample variance makes $(n-1)S^2/S^2=n-1$ identically, erasing the comparison to an unknown population variance. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. Joint normal sampling makes orthogonal linear projections independent; that
   conclusion does not hold for an arbitrary nonnormal sample.

</details>

A chi-squared variable is a sum of independent squared standard normals. When
a sample is centered, one mean direction is projected out; the resulting
variance statistic has $n-1$ degrees of freedom only under independent normal
sampling. The [Student-$t$ distribution](student-t-distribution.qmd) next
combines this variance component with a standardized sample mean.
